messages.body_plain:
Hello fellow S-Plus users;

        I am running S-Plus Academic version 6.2 under Windows 
2000 Professional, and am an S-Plus neophyte.  What I want to do 
is: 

(1) randomly split a data set into a "training set" (say, 2/3 of the 
data) and a "test"set (1/3 of the data); 

(2) fit a model (in this particular instance, a discriminant function, but 
it could in principle be any model) to the training set;

(3) use the fitted model to predict the membership of each 
observation in the  test set;

(4) calculate the (raw) misclassification rates for the test set; 

(5) repeat (1) - (4) for N random splittings of the original data set; 
and

N trials.

Any/all assistance would be much appreciated.

The misclassification rate is an improper scoring rule, i.e., it is
optimized by a bogus model.  It can even increase when an important
variable is added to the model.  I suggest you use a proper scoring rule
or a measure of pure discrimination (e.g., ROC area).  If you want to do
this with the logistic model you can use the Design library ( builtin to
S-Plus) and its lrm and validate functions to get cross-validated indexes
or better to use the bootstrap.

out at the WSL and the PhD degree will be granted by the Department of 
Mathematics (Seminar for Statistics), Swiss Federal Institute of 
Technology (ETHZ), Zurich.

in Switzerland. The head office, where the student will be working, is

http://www.ethrat.ch/content.asp?lng=e&IDpge=1|1 .

data from palaeo-ecology. The work will involve methodological developments 
as well as data applications.

very interdisciplinary atmosphere and have strong background in Statistics 
or Mathematics, with Master's degree in one of these or a related field.

Dear all,

I am trying to do a regression on serial autocorralated data using the
GLS function.

I am interested in analysing phenological plant data (time for fruit
development, % of trees with flowers etc) vs. variables of climate.

My doubts are:

(1) If I fit a model with serial data, but did not detect autocorrelation
exploring the residuals, can I use a common lm() function?

(2) How autocorrelated must the residuals to be (using acf()) in order we
to consider it as autocorrelated?

(3) I could not to find the Durbin-Watson statistic in s-plus. Is it
implemented in S-plus?

Also, I'd like to show you an example I tried to analyse:

For my "tests" I am using a simple model "development ~
temperature".

Looking at the Venables & Ripley
2002 examples, I calculated the acf() for both variables
separately and found:

>
acf(ts(test.gls$development))

> ACF(test.gls.develop)

 3   2  0.96438311

 4   3  0.92063502

 5   4  0.86486571

ACFs were higher than the previous model and the residual plot showed a
strong positive slope pattern!!!

Could you please to help me with some comments and tips???

Many thanks in advance...

rodrigo

São Paulo University - Brazil

messages.subject: Re: order() syntax question
messages.body_plain:
What you want is probably something like:

mat[order(mat[,"a"], -mat[,"b"]),]

order() is sorting the vector, so reversing the order _before_ doesn't help.
If you just want to order by column "b", then mat[rev(order(mat[,"b"])),]
would have worked; i.e., you want to reverse the output of order(), not the
input.

Andy

Thanks for the question.  Using the interaction would be a more 
appropriate response to your question.  The "x+factor(z)" formulation 
assumes that the correlation is the same for different levels of z, but 
it might be different overall due to mixing subpopulations with 
different means.  For what you want, you should group the interaction 
with the main effect of z in the anova as follows:

> set.seed(1)
> DF <- data.frame(x = 1:12, z = rep(letters[1:3], 4), y = rnorm(12))
> fit0 <- lm(y ~ x, DF)
> fitz <- lm(y ~ x * z, DF)
> anova(fit0, fitz)
Analysis of Variance Table

Response: y

2 x * z         6 7.844045 +z+x:z  4  1.390257 0.2658559 0.8897605

for the joint distribution of repeated measures and event times. Statistics 
in Medicine, 16, 239--257.

subject to dropout. Statistical Modeling, 1,

I assume you are using S-PLUS 6.x on Windows (although it would have been 
nice of you to save me the effort of inferring that).

`structure' is just the S4 class of an object with attributes.  What you 
have probably is a matrix already: the issue is that don't want the extra 
attributes na.omit has added to confuse the object explorer.

The real solution is for Insightful to do something more intelligent with 
objects of class "structure".  Meanwhile, I did an experiment.

A <- matrix(c(1:11, NA), 4, 3)
AA <- na.omit(A)
class(AA) # structure
attr(AA, "na.message") <- NULL
class(AA) # matrix

You can change the filtering of the right panel in an object explorer 
to include "structure", but that will not help as Edit.data refuses to 
accept matrices with attributes.

So

attr(AA, "na.message") <- NULL

seems the way forward.

You can build the t-test directly from the means & variance using 
rowMeans and rowVars:

set.seed(1)
dims <- c(100, 3, 2)
a <- array(rnorm(prod(dims)), dim=dims)
b <- array(rnorm(prod(dims)), dim=dims)

# for loop
t1 <- proc.time()
mt <- mp <- array(NA, dim=dims[1:2])
for(i in 1:dims[1]) {
  for(j in 1:dims[2]) {
    tt <- t.test(a[i, j, ], b[i, j, ])
    mt[i, j] <- tt$statistic
    mp[i, j] <- tt$p.value
  }
}
t2 <- proc.time()

t3 <- proc.time()
ma <- rowMeans(a, dims = 2)
mb <- rowMeans(b, dims = 2)
ssa <- rowVars(a, SumSquares = TRUE, dims = 2)
ssb <- rowVars(b, SumSquares = TRUE, dims = 2)
s <- sqrt((ssa + ssb)/(2 * dims[3] - 2))
tarr <- (ma - mb)/s
ptarr <- 2 * (1 - pt(abs(tarr), 2 * dims[3] - 2))
ptarr <- array(ptarr, dim = dims[1:2])
t4 <- proc.time()

As Spencer indicates in his reply the problem is that the variables
xx0, xx1, yy0, etc. are not accessible during the evaluation of
garch.  If you evaluate the individual lines at the top level in the
interpreter then these variables are visible.

Assuming that garch has a 'data' argument (I'm not familiar with the
garch arguments and I don't have easy access to S-PLUS to be able to
check) it would be best to create a data frame with the necessary
variables for the model and pass that.  Rewrite your function like

modfit <- function(yir,yew, ft) {
    yew <- yew[ -length(yew) ]
    yy <- yir-ft
    xx <- yew-ft
 
    n <- length(xx)
    dat <- data.frame(xx0 = xx[2:n], yy0 = yy[2:n], xx1 = xx[ -n ])
    fit <- garch(yy0 ~ xx0+xx1+var.in.mean, ~garch(1,1), data = dat,
                 cond.dist = 'ged')
    summary(fit)
}

messages.subject: Non-Linear Optimizers --- A comparison with a Stochastic Programming problem.
messages.subject_clean: Non-Linear Optimizers --- A comparison with a Stochastic Programming problem.
messages.body_plain:
I've recentally had an opportunity to compare  and stress  the 2  available non-linear optimizers available to S+ and R users: MASS's optim, and Splus's nlminb.  In actual practice, optim far out performed nlminb.

 

 I've been trying to solve a  difficult, 22 variable Stochastic Programming problem, that involves an objective function that includes a nasty barrier function possessing an abrupt, if not discontinuous, first derivative.  The problem involves minimizing the objective function subject to a number of equality constraints.

 

 Because optim  and nlminb  only allow box constraints, I eliminated the equality constraints with use of the "Breaking Stick" parameterization so that the transformed variables only are constrained by box constraints.

 

In use, nlminb  broke down after about 5 minutes of running (on a 3 ghz Win  Xp machine) and gave up with the odd comment that "a singularity had been reached." Probably difficulty computing a numerical derivative or Hessian of the barrier function.

 

 However optim  readily solved the same problem in about  3 minutes utilizing the "L-BFGS-B" method. The comparison of the 2 optimizers was repeated with different input parameters with the same result.  I now have to only solve about 400 more problems to complete the Stochastic sampling...

 

I found the result surprising since I believed that both routines utilized the same standard newton method with a barrier function to account for the box constraints.

 

It would be much better if an interior point routine that could handle inequality constraints was available to Splus and R users, but outside of NUOPT, I can't find one. (Breaking Stick parameteriztions can be unstable because they depend on the order of the variables.)  NUOPT is very touchy, failing to compile many objective functions and it appears to be extremely limited because it does not utilize Splus to program the objective and inequalities. Further in its language the function set is very limited.  Ability to program non-summable objective functions and complicated inequalities is very limited in NUOPT.

 

To effectively solve Stochastic Programming problems the optimizer  should be placed  inside a loop on the stochastic inequality parameters;  use of optim in a loop is  only barely feasible because of its lack of speed.  

 

Any suggestions to help out with this calculational problem would be welcome.

 

 

Paul Lasky

P & B Consultants

Rancho Santa Fe, CA
